meta.title: Who really said "We shall overcome"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Lyndon Johnson quoted it, he didn't coin it. "We shall overcome" is a gospel- and labor-rooted civil-rights anthem that predates his 1965 speech by decades.
meta.ogDescription: Johnson said "And we shall overcome" in 1965 — but he was quoting the civil-rights movement's anthem, a gospel-rooted song traced to Charles Tindley's 1901 hymn.

answer.label: Not Lyndon B. Johnson — a civil-rights anthem he quoted
answer.authorDates: Gospel- & labor-rooted protest song · roots to Charles Tindley’s 1901 hymn · anthem of the U.S. civil-rights movement
answer.sourceLine: Johnson genuinely spoke the words — his March 15, 1965 address to Congress climaxes with “And we shall overcome.” But he was deliberately borrowing the movement’s anthem, not originating it. The line is a folk-gospel protest song that long predates him: it grew from Rev. Charles Tindley’s 1901 hymn “I’ll Overcome Some Day,” was carried by striking tobacco workers, and was published as “We Will Overcome” before Pete Seeger and others reshaped it into “We Shall Overcome.”

source.heading: Where the words actually come from

docMeta.dd: Charles A. Tindley, “I’ll Overcome Some Day” (1901)
“And we shall overcome” — Special Message to Congress, 15 Mar 1965

source.excerpt: Their cause must be our cause too. Because it’s not just Negroes, but really it’s all of us, who must overcome the crippling legacy of bigotry and injustice. And we shall overcome.
trail: The song — not Johnson — is the source: it traces to Charles Tindley’s 1901 hymn, was published as “We Will Overcome” in the late 1940s, and Pete Seeger is credited with changing “will” to “shall,” per Wikipedia’s sourced history.
Johnson really did say “And we shall overcome” on 15 March 1965 — confirmed in the official speech text — but as a borrowing, not a coinage.
A federal court ruled the song’s copyright invalid in 2017 and the publisher agreed it is in the public domain in 2018, per the case summary.
source.excerptNote: Johnson’s peroration on 15 March 1965. The final three words are a direct quotation of the movement’s anthem — the power of the moment came precisely from a Southern president adopting the protesters’ own song.

sourceLink.text: Full speech text — Voices of Democracy

source.rightsNote: Every path to these words lands in the public domain: the gospel root (Tindley’s 1901 hymn) is long PD; the song “We Shall Overcome” was ruled to be in the public domain after a 2017 federal ruling and 2018 settlement; and Johnson’s 1965 speech is a U.S. Government work, PD by statute.

author.name: ‘We Shall Overcome’ (the anthem)
author.heading: A song, not a statesman’s line
author.metaLine: Gospel- & labor-rooted protest song · anthem of the U.S. civil-rights movement
author.bio: “We Shall Overcome” grew out of the African-American church and labor traditions — Rev. Charles Albert Tindley’s 1901 hymn “I’ll Overcome Some Day,” carried by striking Charleston tobacco workers in 1945–46 and taught by Zilphia Horton of the Highlander Folk School. Published as “We Will Overcome,” it was reshaped — Pete Seeger is credited with the “will”-to-“shall” change — and spread by Guy Carawan until it became the unofficial anthem of the civil-rights movement. When Lyndon Johnson reached for its words in 1965, they already belonged to the marchers.

cite.sourceCitation: Lyndon B. Johnson, “Special Message to the Congress: The American Promise,” March 15, 1965 (spoken as “And we shall overcome”). Phrase originates in the anthem “We Shall Overcome,” rooted in Charles A. Tindley, “I’ll Overcome Some Day” (1901) and published as “We Will Overcome,” People’s Songs Bulletin (1948).

misattribution.heading: Who really owns these words
misattribution.intro: Because Johnson’s 1965 address is so famous — it is even titled the “We Shall Overcome” speech — the phrase gets pinned on him as if he authored it. He did not; he quoted a song that was already the heartbeat of the movement.

items.scope: as the author of the phrase
items.why: Johnson spoke “And we shall overcome” to Congress on 15 March 1965 — confirmed in the text — but he was deliberately adopting the protesters’ anthem, which predated him by decades.
The line is inseparable from King and is often attributed to him, but it is a communal folk-gospel song he sang and invoked, not one he wrote, per the documented history.

misattribution.truthLine: The true source is a song with no single author — rooted in Charles Tindley’s 1901 hymn and shaped by Zilphia Horton, Pete Seeger and Guy Carawan — that became the civil-rights movement’s anthem, as traced in Wikipedia’s sourced account.

context.heading: Why the moment mattered
lead: When President Johnson ended his voting-rights address with the movement’s own anthem — eight days after the “Bloody Sunday” beatings in Selma — it landed as an extraordinary act of alignment: a Southern president answering marchers in their own words. Watching on television, Martin Luther King Jr. reportedly wept.

That power depended entirely on the phrase not being Johnson’s. He was returning the movement’s song to it from the podium — which is exactly why crediting the words to him inverts what made the moment historic.
context.pull: He wasn’t coining a slogan. He was handing the marchers back their own anthem.
